title: Septic Pumping with Your Inspection | NC Septic Inspector
description: Septic inspection and pumping in one visit in Western NC. Inspection first, a permitted pumping company empties the tank, then it's evaluated empty.

@graph.name: Septic Inspection with Pumping Arranged
@graph.serviceType: Septic inspection with pumping scheduled for the same visit
@graph.description: A point-of-sale septic inspection with a permitted pumping company scheduled for the same visit, so the tank is evaluated before and after pumping. The pumping company bills the client directly; the scheduling fee is disclosed up front.

mainEntity.name: Do I have to pump the tank for a septic inspection?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The inspection can be done without pumping; the report then carries the statement the state rules require when a client declines to have the tank pumped at inspection. Pumping gives a better look at the tank itself.
You do, directly, at the pumping company's rate. The inspector does not mark up their work or take a referral fee. The scheduling fee is separate, quoted when you book, and shown on the agreement.

mainEntity.name: Should the seller pump the septic tank before listing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not before an inspection. Pump it at the inspection, after the water level and flow have been evaluated. With a pre-listing inspection the pumping receipt becomes part of the disclosure package.

mainEntity.name: Can pumping hide a septic problem?

acceptedAnswer.text: Pumping a day or two before the inspection can. The inspector then sees a near-empty tank and can't judge the water level or whether the drain field is accepting effluent. The order that works is inspect, then pump, then evaluate the empty tank.

mainEntity.name: What if the pumping company finds something?

acceptedAnswer.text: It goes in the inspection report with photos. If the condition warrants it, the report refers you to the county health department or a certified contractor. The inspector does not do repairs.
